Considerate ergo et inquirite quaeque utilia, quaeque [1102A] opportuna et usibus necessaria. Considerate autem non solum bona, sed et mala, commoda et incommoda, munimenta et pericula. Considerate ergo terram et urbem Jericho. Considerate urbem, munitionum firmitatem, hostiumque multitudinem, ut scire possimus quomodo oporteat obsidionem ordinare, qualiter oppugnare, contra quales bellum agere. Inspicite ergo terram et urbem. Inspicite terram quam Deus fecit, et urbem quam humana inventio instituit. Discutite bonum quod Deus creavit ad bonum nostrum, et malum quod homo invenit in malum suum. Considerate terram et urbem, naturam et consuetudinem. Distinguite bonum creationis et malum corruptionis, bonum conditionis et malum consuetudinis. Si naturae bonum cognoscimus, [1102B] scimus quid excolere, quid nutrire, quid multiplicare debeamus. Si morum nostrorum malum perspicimus, quos hostes cavere, quos adversarios oppugnare, quales inimicos interficere oporteat non dubitamus. Ecce quales exploratores debemus ante ingressum nostrum praemittere, ut sciamus contra quae mala cavenda, et ad quae bona agenda debeamus vigilare. Qui tales exploratores ante faciem suam praemittit, errorum devia minime formidabit.

## CAPUT XV. *Quid sit meditationis, et quid sit contemplationis.*

Sed ille virtutum exercitus secure incedit, sibique de viae certitudine nihil diffidit, quem exploratorum [1102C] sagacitas instruit. et arcae ordinata antecessio in suo itinere dirigit. Parum nobis sit ante Hebraeorum turbam exploratores dirigere; faciamus et arcam nostram post exploratorum vestigia faciem nostram praecedere. Primum est faciendorum rationem meditationum nostrarum exploratione perquirere et invenire, et postea tandem oportet in contemplationem adducere, ut possimus notam, et promptam, et familiarem habere. Contemplatio pertinet ad arcae evectionem, sicut meditatio ad explorationem. Aliud est contemplationis, aliud est meditationis. Meditationis est perscrutari occulta, contemplationis est admirari perspicua. Siquidem meditatio est occultae veritatis studiosa investigatio. Contemplatio est perspicuae veritatis jucunda admiratio. Quae autem occulta sunt, [1102D] solent ad manifestationem prodire, modo ex propria meditatione, modo ex divina revelatione. Ubi ergo revelationis gratiam praesentem habemus, meditationis officio non egemus. Ubi autem divina revelatio defuerit, mens humana, nec mirum, ad meditationis studium ex necessitate recurrit, et quasi ad exploratorum officia refugit. Sed quidquid mens humana de morum instructione poterit meditationum exploratione cognoscere, debet iterum in contemplationem adducere, et in eorum certitudinem et desiderium animum roborare. Sed cum meditationis adinventio in contemplationem adducitur, quid aliud quam via prius explorata ad arcae evectionem repetitur, ut virtutum turma absque deviationis [1103A] suspicione secure subsequatur? Per meditationem itaque agitur, ut quidquid utiliter fieri debeat non ignoretur. Sed et contemplatio illud efficere solet, ut adinventa veritas memoriae tenacius inhaereat, et desiderium acrius inflammet. Per meditationem [1104A] ergo ad bonum instruimur, et per contemplationem in bono solidamur. Haec est ratio, ut arbitror, cur debeamus profectuum nostrorum viam, et meditationis exploratione, et intellectualis arcae processione praetentare.

## TRACTATUS TERTIUS. *Hucusque de boni promotione, abhinc de ejusdem confirmatione.*



## CAPUT PRIMUM.

[1103A]

Libet et illud considerare quid sit quod Dominus jubet de Jordanis medio, de loco ubi steterunt sacerdotum [1103B] pedes, lapides colligere, et in loco castrorum ponere, et alios undecunque collectos in priori loco reponere. Quaeramus ergo quis ille sit locus, quo sacerdotum pedes tempore faciendi miraculi subsistunt, vel quo itidem loco post celebratum miraculum castra figenda sunt. Quis dubitet supra humanam virtutem esse Jordanem retroire, et aquarum congeriem in unam molem consurgere? Quis, quaeso, nisi mente excidat, tam stupendum miraculum de sua virtute praesumat? Ubi ergo debet animus sub tantae rei exspectatione spem suam figere, nisi in fiducia divinae magnificentiae? Tutus stationis locus et magnae securitatis, praesumptio de adjutorio divinae pietatis. Sed est alius locus loco huic valde dissimilis, subreptio videlicet diffidentiae et desperationis. [1103C] Locus sane horridus, plenus timoris, plenus sollicitudinis, et qualem denique decet castris munire, vallo cingere, excubiis circumdare, eo quod non sit tutum propter imminentia pericula in ulteriora procedere. Illum primum tempore divinae visitationis, istum autem tempore probationis incurrimus. Solet enim divinae pietatis dispensatio hominem cum sua visitatione confortare, et iterum vario tentationum genere probare: *Visitas,* inquit Job, *eum diluculo, et subito probas illum [n: (Job VII)]*. Ecce duos locos assignavimus, unum confidentiae, alterum diffidentiae; unum quo solent divina miracula contingere, alterum quo oportet castra figere. Qui confidunt in Domino mutabunt fortitudinem, assument [1103D] pennas ut aquilae, current et non deficient. Nonne totum supra hominem est fortitudinem mutare, juxta aquilae similitudinem volare, currere et non deficere? Sed hoc tamen soli ipsi possunt qui de Domini pietate, non de sua fortitudine praesumunt. Sic Petrus super undas currere potuit quandiu confidentiae locum spei pede tenuit [n: (Matth. XIV)]. Sed postquam coepit hunc suae securitatis locum deserere, non potuit eum unda in superioribus suis amplius librare. Vides quomodo ventus validus superveniens de loco confidentiae ad locum eum diffidentiae dejecit, eo quod Dominus juxta morem suum visitasset eum diluculo, et subito probasset illum. Sic filii Israel post factum visumque miraculum, venerunt ad locum castrorum.

## CAPUT II. *De confirmatione mentis in bono et obduratione mentis in malo.*

[1104A]

[1104B]Assignavimus differentiam locorum, videamus et duo genera lapidum. Puto esse unum genus lapidum bonorum, puto esse et aliud malorum lapidum. Ad lapides bonos pertinet quaelibet mentis confirmatio in bono; ad lapides autem malos, quaelibet mentis obduratio in malo. Quid tibi videtur? Soliditas, stabilitas, firmitas, gravitas et multa in hunc modum, nonne tibi videntur quamdam in se lapidum similitudinem trahere, et pro similitudinis jure sibi tale nomen juste vindicare? Quid dicimus de cordis duritia, tenacia vel obstinatia? quid de asperitate, austeritate et crudelitate? Nonne sibi lapidis nomen defendunt quae in se lapidum similitudinem trahunt? Sed priores illi pertinent ad lapides bonos, sicut et isti posteriores ad lapides malos. [1104C] Sed puto non esse ejusdem facilitatis bonos vel malos lapides invenire, eo quod difficilius sit bonos lapides quam malorum copiam reperire. Omne enim pretiosum rarum. Boni ergo colliguntur de medio Jordanis, mali autem de quibuscunque locis. De illis Scriptura, ubi eos quaerere vel invenire oporteat, manifeste designat; de his autem adinventionis locum determinare quasi superfluum judicat.



## CAPUT III. *De malo praesumptionis seu desperationis.*

Sed illud videtur mirum magnaque admiratione dignum quod jubemur bonos lapides de bono loco collectos in malo loco reponere, malos autem lapides [1104D] undecunque collectos in bono loco aggregare. Locus bonus praesumptio confidentiae, locus malus desperatio diffidentiae. Sed tamen debemus in loco confidentiae congregare lapides malos, et in loco diffidentiae congregare lapides bonos. In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et congregasti lapides malos in loco bono, et in die malorum ne immemor sis bonorum, et congregasti lapides bonos in loco malo. Quid enim est lapides bonos de medio Jordanis (de loco videlicet facti prodigii) colligere, nisi statum mentis qualis tempore divinae visitationis fuerit diligenter retractare, et cujus firmitatis secundum unamquamque virtutem exstiterit subtiliter investigare, memoriaeque commendando quasi quemdam testimonii tumulum erigere? Sed nunquam talium lapidum [1105A] copiam habemus, nisi prius divinae visitationis et inspirationis gratiam acceperimus. Testatur hoc qui dicit: *Sine me nihil potestis facere [n: (Joan. XV)]*; ergo nec lapides bonos est uspiam colligere nisi ex ejus operatione. Sed malorum lapidum innumeram multitudinem facile invenimus, quos ex tota vita nostra copiose et ad manum colligimus. Quid ergo opus fuit horum locum designare, quos ubertim possumus undecunque congregare? Cogitet ergo quisque cujus duritiei, cujus obstinationis fuerit, quoties eum divina gratia deseruit, sibique ipsi reliquit: et hoc faciens malorum lapidum tumulum erexit. In hunc itaque modum possumus tumulos erigere, et diversos e diverso constituere, hinc unum de lapidibus bonis, illinc alium de lapidibus malis. Bonorum lapidum [1105B] sibi congeriem instituit, qui dixit: *In aeternum non obliviscar justificationes tuas, quia in ipsis vivificasti me [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Malorum lapidum tumulum erexerat, cum dicebat: *Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco, et peccatum meum contra me est semper [n: (Psal. L)]*.

## CAPUT IV. *Quomodo ex malorum nostrorum recordatione oporteat praesumptionem reprimere.*

Sic et tu cum locum confidentiae teipsum tenere praesenseris, et meritis tuis altiora praesumere perspexeris, memento statim quid aliquando fueris, et ad malorum lapidum congeriem oculos reflectens teipsum in humilitate custodis. Bonum est sane [1105C] praesumere, non de tua tamen fortitudine, sed de Domini pietate. Ad hoc malorum lapidum in loco bono congregatio cuique valeat, ut per malorum suorum memoriam nunquam de suis viribus praesumat. Ut ergo discat unusquisque praesumere, non de seipso, sed de Domino, semper sibi in praesumptionis loco occurrat malorum suorum recordatio: illa sane praesumptionis fiducia Dominum placat, et magnalia impetrat, quam humilitas commendat. Qui confidunt in Domino sicut mons Sion. Sic econtrario abominabilis est illa praesumptionum fiducia quam generat superbia. Non enim salvatur rex per multam virtutem suam, et gigas non salvabitur in multitudine virtutis suae. Maledictus ergo homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium [1105D] suum: erit enim sicut myricae in deserto, et non saturabitur cum venerit aestas, quam utilis ergo, putamus, erit in hujusmodi loco illa quam praescripsimus malorum lapidum congregatio, vitiorumque recordatio, quae nos poterit custodire ab hoc exsecrabili superbiae typo, et protegere ab hujusmodi maledicto.

## CAPUT V. *Quomodo ex bonorum nostrorum recordatione oporteat desperationem repellere.*

Sic sane periculo imminente, tentatione superveniente, cum praesenseris animum tuum desperatione tangi, et ad diffidentiae locum dejici, et ad praefinitum castrorum locum devolvi, debes bonorum lapidum tumulum praesentem habere, et ad virtutum [1106A] praeteritarum memoriam oculos reflectere, et ex earum recordatione spei tuae fiduciam reformare. Sic Job rebus nudatus, filiis viduatus, ulcere percussus, cum se in loco castrorum deprehensum cerneret, et desperationis malo se pulsari praesentiret, ut diffidentiae malum temperaret, ad bonorum lapidum acervum recurrit, et ex bonorum recordatione castra sua undique munit, et desperationis insultus fortiter repellit, cum dicit: *Oculus fui caeco, et pes claudo; pater eram pauperum, et causam quam nesciebam diligenter investigabam. Conterebam molas iniqui, et dentibus illius auferebam praedam [n: (Job XXIX)]*. Sic et Ezechias sub necessitatis articulo ad hujusmodi lapidum munimina recurrebat, cum de vita diffideret, et ex bonorum actuum [1106B] suorum repraesentatione, Domini misericordiam provocabat, precumque suarum obtentu, diffidentiae pericula propulsabat: *Memento,* inquit, *Domine, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et corde perfecto, et quod bonum est in oculis tuis fecerim [n: (IV Reg. XX)]*. Debemus itaque et nos promptum et familiare haberi sub omni tempore tentationis, anteactorum bonorum memoriam praesentem tenere et cum hanc consuetudinem in continuum usum duxerimus, quasi lapides bonos, et juxta divinum documentum electos in loco castrorum collocavimus. Nihil enim aliud est electos lapides in unum locum congregare, nisi divinae confirmationis et corroborationis qualitates diligenter retractare, memoriaeque [1106C] commendare, et nihil aliud est eos in loco castrorum fixisse, nisi hujusmodi memoriam in omni tentationis articulo firmiter assuevisse.

## CAPUT VI. *De duodceim principalibus virtutibus in quibus solidandus est animus.*

Hos autem de medio Jordanis alveo per Dei virtutem siccato, et ad numerum duodecim tribuum colligimus, quando statum mentis nostrae, qualis sub divinae visitationis tempore fuerit, diligenter discutimus, et quales tunc temporis in unaquaque principalium virtutum, juxta aliquid fuerimus, subtiliter exquirimus. Hoc est enim singulos de singulis tribubus homines suum lapidem tollere, quantae firmitatis, juxta aliquid ad singulas virtutes per [1106D] aspirationis gratiam aliquando exstiterit, veraciter invenisse. Quid autem de duodecim filiis Jacob sentiamus, ex quibus originem trahunt hae duodecim tribus, alio loco jam diximus. Per Ruben et Simeonem intelligimus timorem et compunctionem; per Levi, spem; per Judam, charitatem; per Issachar, jucunditatem; per Zabulon, severitatem; in Gad intelligitur abstinentia; in Aser, patientia; in Dan et Nephtalim, circumspectio et speculatio; in Joseph et Benjamin, discretio et invisibilium contemplatio. Horum autem rationem hoc loco ostendere jam volumus, de quibus quod nobis rectius videbatur alias jam diximus. Sed qui ex tali sobole semen suum in duodecim tribubus multiplicatum esse confidit discat quales lapides de medio Jordanis tollere debuerit, [1107A] cum hanc virtutum progeniem usque ad ejus transitum promoverit. Recolat ergo quid roboris, quid fortitudinis vel firmitatis ad divinae aspirationis afflatum se senserit hausisse, hoc est et lapides electos de loco determinato tulisse. Sed ut per singulos de singulis tribubus homines haec lapidum electio fiat, hanc considerationis suae operam per singulas quas distinximus virtutes exerceat, et lapidum suorum numerum usque in duodenarium extendat. Cogitet ergo quisquis cupit post Jordanis conversionem hoc Dominicum praeceptum implere; cogitet, inquam, sub tempore divinae visitationis cujus vigoris fuerit juxta aliquid in unaqualibet virtute. Cogitet quanta soliditas tunc temporis ei fuerit in timore, quanta gravitas in compunctione, [1107B] quanta stabilitas in spe, quanta integritas in charitate, quanta maturitas in jucunditate, quanta asperitas in severitate. Cogitet quam austerus fuerit in abstinentia, quam robustus in patientia, quam sollicitus in circumspectione, quam assiduus in speculatione, quam certus in discretione, quam quietus in contemplatione. Cum autem haec omnia plene perspexerit memoriaeque mandaverit, tumulum qualem oportuit erexit. Infiniti negotii esset, et quod nemo omnino explere potuisset, si juberet Dominus omnes de omnibus tribubus lapidem suum tollere, eo quod nemo sufficeret seipsum digne pensare, qualis sit ad omnia, non dicam in omni, sed una solummodo qualibet virtute. Sufficit ergo unum [1107C] aliquod praeclarum et insigne aestus sui desiderium per omnes has quas determinavimus virtutes segregare, talisque memoriae usum firmare et in ejusmodi recordatione sub omni diffidentiae periculo contra desperationis malum pugnare. Facile enim animum suum quantumlibet dejectum, quantalibet tentatione pulsatum, ad spem divinae miserationis statumque confidentiae reparat: qui qualis aliquando ex divina operatione fuerit, ad memoriam revocat. Omnino et absque dubio libenter se exercet in tali studio, cui datum est nosse quid valeat, vel quod utilis sit haec hujusmodi lapidum studiosa collectio.



## CAPUT VII. *De soliditate timoris.*

[1107D]Quam utilem, quaeso, putamus illum lapidem quem primo loco posuimus, soliditatem videlicet timoris per quem mens fundatur in solido humilitatis. Quantum autem valeat Dominica illa sententia probat, quae dicit: *Super quem requiescet Spiritus meus, nisi super humilem, et quietum, et trementem sermones meos? [n: (Isa. LVI.)]* Hic est lapis offensionis et petra scandali, nisi forte dubites hunc esse lapidem quem reprobaverunt aedificantes, et factus est in caput anguli. Superbae etenim mentes, et suam justitiam statuere volentes, nil solent molestius pati, nihil amplius indignari quam apparere despecti et viles videri.

## CAPUT VIII. *De gravitate compunctionis.*

[1108A]

Sed et secundum lapidem, qui dictus est gravitas compunctionis, apud Jeremiam puto posse reperiri, qui petivit capiti suo aquas ut lugeat interfectos populi sui [n: (Jer. V)], et datum ei non dubito ab eo qui convertit petram in stagna aquarum et rupes in fontem aquarum. Hanc eamdem petram apud Petrum puto inveniri posse, eo quod tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus egressus sit foras, et flevit amare, percutiens bis silicem, et egressae sunt aquae largissimae, et factum est irriguum superius, et irriguum inferius.

## CAPUT IX. *De spei longanimitate.*

[1108B]Tertiam petram, quae est longanimitas spei, apud Job non dubito posse reperiri, de qua sibi fundebat rivos olei, unde et lenibat dolores corporis sui. Sperabat enim usque ad mane inter tot damna, dolorumque vulnera, nunquam exhaustus oleo spei suae, nusquam diffidens de unctione divinae misericordiae: *Etiamsi occiderit me,* inquiens, *in ipso sperabo [n: (Job XIII)]*.

## CAPUT X. *De charitatis integritate.*

Quartam itidem apud Petrum petram invenio, cui dictum esse non dubitamus a Domino: *Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam [n: (Matth. XVI)]*, eo quod diligeret Christum Domini ex [1108C] toto corde suo, et ex tota anima sua, et ex tota mente sua, veraciter agnoscens quod ipse esset Christus Filius Dei vivi. Ubi, obsecro, invenitur charitatis integritas si eam apud Petrum non reperias, qui coram cordium inspectore audet profiteri et dicere: *Domine, tu scis quia amo te? [n: (Joan. XXI.)]*

## CAPUT XI. *De maturitate jucunditatis.*

Quintam autem petram apud populum illum esse dubitare quis audeat, quem Propheta Domini inter caetera prophetiae dogmata beatificat? *Beatus,* inquit, *populus qui scit jubilationem [n: (Psal. LXXXVIII)]*. Beatos utique esse quis neget, quos Dominus cibavit adipe frumenti, et de petra melle saturavit eos: jucunditatem etenim et exsultationem thesaurizavit [1108D] super eos. Animadvertis, ut arbitror, quale sit etiam hunc lapidem inter caeteros possidere, qui fluit jucunditatis melle, et satiat intrantem in gaudium Domini sui interna dulcedine. Quale, quaeso, erit quoties opportunum fuerit de petra melle saturari, et de torrente voluptatis in via bibere et inebriari? Hic est quintus ille, ut dictum est, lapis, qui dictus est maturitas jucunditatis. Nil ergo levitatis habeat, nil ei caducum, nil carnale sapiat, ad magnam autem maturitatis gravitatem animum componat, qui solum hoc esurit et sitit, quod de hoc lapide manat.

## CAPUT XII. *De asperitate severitatis.*

Sed ille, ut arbitror, dimicabat in lapide sexto, [1109A] cui dictum est a Domino: *Ecce dedi faciem tuam valentiorem faciebus eorum, et frontem tuam duriorem frontibus eorum, ut adamantem et ut silicem dedi faciem tuam [n: (Ezech. III)]*. Conterebat ergo Jeremias exasperantem domum Israel in adamante et silice, eo quod esset attrita fronte et duro corde, stansque in porta domus Domini, annuntiabat eis scelera eorum, verba eorum non timens, nec vultus eorum. Hunc lapidem tenet in manibus rex ille fortis et potens in praelio, in quo dejectus est fortis armatus, et vir bellicosus ab adolescentia sua. Praevaluit enim David in Philisthaeum in funda et lapide in nomine Domini. Vides certe qualibus armis ille adolescentulus et contemptus et statura pusillus dejecerit Goliam gigantem immanissimum, eo quod [1109B] doctus esset a Domino doctas habere manns ad praelium et digitos suos ad bellum. Habebat sane arma non carnalia, sed potentia a Deo ad destructionem munitionum, et erat in eis pugnans et destruens omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus scientiam Dei, et in captivitatem redigens omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Super omnes enim docentes se intellexit, et idcirco fiducialiter annuntiavit justitiam Domini in Ecclesia magna, sicut et ipse de seipso de praeterito perhibuit, et de futuro promittit: *Annuntiavi,* inquit, *justitiam tuam in Ecclesia magna, ecce labia mea non prohibebo: Domine, tu scisti [n: (Psal. XXXIX)]*. In promptu itaque habes ulcisci omnem inobedientiam, arguebat elatos, corripiebat inquietos, et in asperrimae increpationis lapide et correptionis [1109C] asperitate dejiciebat veritatis adversarios. Et cum esset vir mitissimus in populo suo et mansuetissimus: *Memento,* inquiens, *Domine, David, et omnis mansuetudinis ejus [n: (Psal. CXXXI)]*; cum esset, inquam, tantae mansuetudinis, nihilominus tamen in matutino interficiebat omnes peccatores terrae, ut disperderet de civitate Domini omnes operantes iniquitatem.

## CAPUT XIII. *De austeritate abstinentiae.*

Septimum lapidem diximus esse austeritatem abstinentiae. In hac petra pater Samson obtulit Domino holocaustum, et obtinuit gignere de sterili virum fortissimum virorum, ad ignominiam gentium, [1109D] et gloriam plebis suae Israel [n: (Judic. XIII)]. Puduit sane eum tandem aliquandiu pavisse sterilem, et quae non parit, et ulterius noluit, sicut nec debuit, debitor esse carnis, ut secundum carnem viveret, sed castigans corpus suum, et in servitutem redigens, haedinasque carnes in abstinentiae petra immolans, jusque carnium cum carnibus ipsis accepto coelitus igne consumens, fluxasque corporis restringens noluit de caetero ire post concupiscentias suas. Sicque, impetu carnis edomito, impetum spiritus roboravit, qui carnis infirmitate fit fortior.



## CAPUT XIV. *De robore patientiae.*

Post hos lapides sequitur robur patientiae: quem [1110A] lapidem me recolo octavo loco annumerasse. Ecce lapis fortissimus, omniumque durissimus. Hunc lapidem tenet in manibus coelestis militiae signifer ille protomartyr Stephanus, et factus est ei turris fortitudinis a facie inimici. In hoc lapide lapidum se prementium sustinuit fortiter ictus, nec timuit lapidantium manus, nec eorum impetum, qui stridebant dentibus in eum [n: (Act. VII)]. O lapis fortis et durus, sed dulcedine plenus! O pectus robustissimum, sed pietate plenum! Miraris quilibet audis quomodo in patientia sua possedit animam suam, sed mirari potius debuisses quomodo animus sub tanta persecutionis amaritudine non amiserit dulcedinem suam. Ab inimicis premebatur, et pro inimicis precabatur. Sustinebat saevitiam humanam, et [1110B] suspiciebat gloriam divinam: *Ecce,* inquit, *video coelos apertos, et Jesum stantem a dextris virtutis Dei [n: (ibid.)]*. In terris premebatur, et de coelis consolabatur. Affligebatur ex illata miseria, afficiebatur ex inolita misericordia, gratulabatur ex inspecta gloria. Ecce sub uno eodemque tempore videbat inferius unde compateretur, videbat superius unde jucundaretur. Ecce quomodo de eodem pectore manabat pietas cum jucunditate, jucunditas cum pietate. Ecce quomodo de eodem vase manat oleum cum melle, oleum pietatis cum melle jucunditatis. Quae, quaeso, est ista in lapide isto olei et mellis impermista confusio et inconfusa permistio? Miror si non miraris quomodo pugnator fortis sub uno eodemque momento sugebat mel de petra oleumque de saxo durissimo. [1110C] Mira virtus patientiae, et quis digne penset pretium hujus petrae, quae in tanta copia distillat oleum cum melle? Quanta, quaeso, olei et mellis copia inesse deprehenditur, ubi misericordia nulla malitia minuitur, ubi dulcedo nullo dolore attenuatur? Imo mirum in modum crescit ex dolore delectatio, et ex passione compassio. Martyr sane cum lapidaretur, magis miserebatur inimicis suis quam membris suis. Positis enim genibus orabat, dicens: *Domine, ne statuas illis hoc peccatum, quia nesciunt quid faciunt [n: (ibid.)]*. Ecce quoad positionem genuum effusum est oleum, et de caetero velut oleum effusum factum est nomen suum. Siquidem ad miserationem inimici facta est effusio olei, intantum ut [1110D] adolescens, qui eminus sedebat, respersus sit ex odore unguenti. Incurvato namque corpore et inclinato capite, coepit oleum effluere, et factum est sicut unguentum in capite, et descendit in oram vestimenti ejus qui vestimenta servabat. Velociter ergo surgens, qui diu sederat in tenebrosis et in umbra mortis coepit currere in odorem unguentorum, exsultansque ut gigas ad currendam viam suam, quocunque erat impetus Spiritus, illic gradiebatur, et de caetero factus est Christi bonus odor omni loco.

## CAPUT XV. *De sollicitudine circumspectionis.*

Nonam petram invenio apud Ezechiam, invenio eam et apud amici sponsam, sponsique amicam, cui [1111A] dicitur in Canticis: *Surge, amica mea, speciosa mea, et veni, columba mea, in foraminibus petrae, in caverna maceriae [n: (Cant. II)]*. Sic et Ezechias ad sponsae similitudinem quietem eligens, secretumque captans, sedensque in foraminibus petrae, seu etiam caverna maceriae, sicut pullus hirundinis, sic clamabat, meditabatur ut columba: O quis mihi dabit pennas sicut columbae, et volabo, et requiescam, si forte possim evolare in id loci, ubi passer invenit sibi domum, et turtur nidum ubi reponat pullos suos! Ubi, quaeso, quidquam tuti reperietur, si in foraminibus hujusmodi petrae non invenietur, ubi studiosa praemeditatio quaecunque pericula, antequam eveniant, praevidet, et ventura praeveniens, ex praeteritis futura colligit, et de dubiis rebus non dubios [1111B] eventus saepe praenoscit? Quid enim est aliud circumspectio, nisi circumstantium malorum sollicita sagaxque perscrutatio? Ad hanc pertinet praeteritorum malorum retractatio, praesentium consideratio, futurorum praemeditatio, ut secundum nomen suum veraciter sit circumspectio. Hujus assiduitas hominem cautum efficit, et quantum possibile est, tutum reddit.

## CAPUT XVI. *De assiduitate speculationis.*

Decimus lapis dictus est assiduitas speculationis. Jacob declinans a malo, dansque locum irae, dum peregre proficiscitur festinans, ne fuga sua fieret hieme aut Sabbato, hunc lapidem in itinere invenit, [1111C] inventumque capiti suo supposuit, ne non haberet ubi caput suum reclinaret, dum in via obdormiret [n: (Gen. XXVIII)]. In hoc lapide in pace, in idipsum obdormit et requiescit, et in itinere requiem invenit, quam nec in cubiculis stratisque purpureis invenire possunt qui mollibus vestiuntur, et in domibus regum sunt. Reclinato itaque capite, Jacob in hoc lapide, clausisque oculis concupiscentiae (quos apertos legimus in primo parente), dum in hoc reclinatorio alta quiete sopitur, dum exteriorum omnium libenter obliviscitur, animus ejus ad interiora evigilat, videtque quae prius vigilans et videns videre non poterat. Scala usque in coelum porrecta, ante ejus oculos erigitur, Dominusque innixus scalae conspicitur, ut per invisibilem formam, invisibiliumque figuram, [1111D] in intellectibilium intelligentiam, speculantis animus sublevetur. Felix cui visibilium scientia fit scala ad invisibilia cognoscenda. Pulchrum spectaculum videre hujus scalae scalaria modo congruo, proportionabiliterque locata, et usque in summum ordinatae distinctionis continuatione producta, ut per multiplicem creaturarum differentiam, dignitatumque degradationem ordinate distinctam, distincteque ordinatam, paulatim se animus ad superiora promoveat, provectionisque gradibus semper ad altiora conscendat, donec invisibilia Dei a creatura mundi, per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta conspiciantur, et Dominus innixus scalae videatur. Quis, quaeso, hoc, nisi in hoc reclinatorio dormiens videret, quis hoc evigilans efficeret, ut ascensionis suae [1112A] scalam usque in coelum protenderet, et visibilium speculationi speculationem invisibilium continuaret? Quid quod in hoc ascensionis tramite angelicae occursionis alludium sponte se ingerit, ut humanae investigationi divina revelatio occurrat? Itaque videntur angeli in hac scala nunc ascendere, nunc vero descendere, et nunc ad summa, nunc ad ima animum erudire, ut in divinis et humanis multa, quae per seipsum non poterat, ex divina revelatione cognoscat. Et possent quidem angeli sine scalae ministerio pro desiderii sui arbitrio, sive in ima descendere, sive ad summa evolare, nec opus esset divinae inspirationi in ulla revelationum suarum manifestatione ullius corporeae similitudinis instrumentum quaerere, nisi vellet nos primo per [1112B] speculum, et in aenigmate, et non statim facie ad faciem videre. Ascendunt itaque angeli in hac similitudinum scala atque descendunt, atque alii post alios modo accedunt, modo discedunt, ut dum multiplicium revelationum alia ingeritur, alia subtrahitur, speculantis animus multiformiter illuminetur, ut quae simul pro intelligentiae suae exiguitate capere non poterat, succedenter et per morarum intervalla sigillatim intelligat. Ecce quid inveniunt, qui in hoc lapide obdormiunt. Felices quibus vertitur in scalam, quod aliis solet esse in ruinam. Felices quibus exteriorum scientia fit scala ascensionis, non ruina dejectionis. Felices quibus scientia illa quae inflat, non est ad inflationem, sed ad inflammationem ejus quae aedificat. Felices quibus temporalium pulchritudo fit [1112C] aeternitatis instigatio. Oportet ergo, ut animadvertis, caput in lapide reclinare, et in hujus speculationis desiderio animum obdurare, et huic studio pertinaciter insistere, qui cupit hanc ascensionis scalam invenire.



## CAPUT XVII. *De certitudine discretionis.*

Certitudinem discretionis undecimum lapidem diximus, quam si diligenter quaerimus, citius apud Paulum invenimus. Tantum siquidem de discretionis dono confidit, tantum de consilii sui certitudine praesumit, ut fidenter consilium det, ubi Dominicum praeceptum non habet: *De virginibus,* inquit, *praeceptum Domini non habeo, consilium autem do (I [1112D] Cor. VII)*. Hinc est quod aliis seipsum in exemplum conversationis proponit, et vitam suam vivendi formam sequacibus ostendit, cum dicit: *Imitatores mei estote, sicut et ego Christi [n: (I Cor. XL)]*. Et recte sane eo quod statuerit Dominus supra petram pedes suos, et direxit gressus suos. Hujusmodi, ut arbitror, lapidibus viatorum illorum via strata erat, de quibus Propheta pro admiratione exclamat: *Quam speciosi pedes evangelizantium pacem, evangelizantium bona! [n: (Rom. X.)]* His, ni fallor, lapidibus magnus ille patriarcha Joseph, quem princeps populorum constituit dominum domus suae, et principem omnis possessionis suae, ut erudiret principes ejus sicut semetipsum, et senes ejus prudentiam doceret. His, inquam, lapidibus plateas Aegypti [1113A] recte creditur stravisse, intantum ut non haberent filii Israel necesse servire in luto et latere omnibus diebus vitae suae. Horum adhuc lapidum penuriam Propheta sustinebat, et sub magna discretionis inopia laborabat, cum adhuc fixus esset in limo profundi, eo quod nondum sibi constaret rati certitudo consilii, intantum ut Domino proclamaret et diceret: *Quandiu ponam consilia in anima mea? [n: (Psal. XVIII.)]* Sed de hoc limi profundo nunquam plene emersisset, nisi hanc, de qua loquimur, petram tandem aliquando invenisset: *In petra,* inquit, *exaltavit, me, et nunc exaltavit caput meum super inimicos meos [n: (Psal. XXVI)]*. Qui de hoc genere lapidum viam sibi non sternit, nunquam munde incedit, nunquam stabiles gressus figit. Qui vult [1113B] ergo firmiter et honeste incedere, debet nil omnino inconsulte agere, et quali debuit lapide constat sibi viam stravisse, et potest secure incedere. Omnia, inquit Sapiens, fac cum consilio, et nunquam poenitebis [n: (Eccle. XXXII)].



## CAPUT XVIII. *De quiete contemplationis.*

Lapidem duodecimum, omniumque novissimum invenire possumus, ut arbitror, apud Dominicum sepulcrum. Dictus est, ut superius est dictum, lapis is tranquillitas contemplationis. De hoc genere lapidum Joseph ille ab Arimathaea sepulcra sibi incidit, sed Jesus in eo mortuus quievit, quia quietem quam prudentia sibi per meditationem quaerit, et per diffinitionem describit, sapientia per contemplationem [1113C] invenit, et per experimentum apprehendit. Semper vera prudentia quaerit, et semper quaerere debet illam quam Christus docuit pacem, ut non turbetur neque formidet. Semper studet ubi talem pacem inveniat, semper nititur ut veram sibi securitatem defendat, sed semper invenit quod de praeterito doleat, quod in praesenti oppugnet, quod in futurum caveat atque pertimescat. Potest ergo animus hanc pacem per prudentiam solerter quaerere, et per meditationem subtiliter investigare, nunquam eam tamen nisi per sapientiam et contemplationis gratiam poterit invenire. Sed, cum coeperit animus per puram intelligentiam semetipsum excedere, et in illam incorporeae lucis claritatem [1113D] totus intrare, et in his quae in intimis videt quemdam intimae suavitatis saporem trahere, et ex eo intelligentiam suam condire, et in sapientiam vertere, intantum in hoc mentis excessu pax illa quae neque turbatur, neque formidat, invenitur atque obtinetur ut fiat silentium in coelo quasi hora dimidia, ita ut contemplantis animus nulla altercantium cogitationum tumultuatione turbetur: nihil omnino invenies, vel quod per desiderium petat, vel per fastidium arguat, vel per odium accuset. Ad summam itaque pacem componitur, qui in hoc lapide sepelitur, qui intra contemplationis tranquillitatem totus colligitur atque concluditur. Neque enim lapis iste sicut ille Jacob soli capiti supponitur, neque sicut ille posterior pedibus substernitur, sed toto [1114A] corpori coaptatur atque applicatur. Hic itaque lapis totum corpus ambit, totum includit, et ab omni parte comprehendit, eo quod pax illa, quae omnem sensum exsuperat, omnem sensum humanum funditus absorbeat, et in divinum quemdam habitum puriorem animae partem felici transfiguratione convertat. Jacet hic corpus sine sensu et motu in hoc Dominico monumento; nihil sensualitas, nihil agit imaginatio, et omnis inferior vis animae proprio interim induitur officio.

Non enim hoc lapideum monumentum (sicut saxeum illud patriarchae Jacob reclinatorium) suscipit corpus vivum, quamvis sopitum, nec recipit corpus nisi mortificatum. Aliud dormire, aliud est obire. Aliud spiritum suum totum in seipsum colligere, [1114B] et aliud est supra se levare et seipsum deserere. Aliud est appetitum coercuisse, exteriorumque curam cordi excidisse atque aliud est ipsum sibi in oblivionem venire. Oportet ergo antequam introire liceat in illud intimae quietis secretum et summae tranquillitatis arcanum; oportet, inquam, ut fiat illa valde gravis et vere mirabilis, non dissolutio animae et corporis, sed alia hac multo mirabilior multoque gloriosior, illa denique, cujus ista est typus, divisio videlicet animae et spiritus. Hanc autem operari in nobis solet sicut testatur Apostolus, vivus ille Dei sermo et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, et pertingens usque ad divisionem animae et spiritus. Quid, quaeso, uspiam creaturarum hac divisione mirabilius cernitur, ubi [1114C] id quod essentialiter unum est atque individuum in seipsum scinditur, et quod simplex in se et sine partibus constat a seipso dividitur atque separatur? Neque enim in homine uno alia essentia est ejus spiritus, atque alia ejus est anima, sed prorsus una eademque simplicisque naturae substantia. Non enim in hoc gemino vocabulo gemina substantia intelligitur; sed, cum ad distinctionem ponitur gemina vis ejusdem essentiae, una superior per spiritum, alia inferior per animam designatur. In hac itaque divisione, anima et quod animale est in imo remanet; spiritus autem et quod spirituale est ad summa evolat. Quod corpulentum atque feculentum quasi corpus emortuum deficit, et recidit in se [1114D] et sub seipsum; quod subtile et defaecatum est quasi spiritus efflatus ascendit, et transcendit intra, et ultra semetipsum. O alta quies, o sublimis requies, ubi omne quod humanitus moveri solet motum omnem amittit, ubi omnis qui tunc est motus divinitus fit, et in Deum transit! Hic ille Spiritus efflatus, et in manus Patris commendatus non, ut ille somniator Jacob, scala indiget, ut ad tertium, ne dicam ad primum, coelum evolet. Quid, quaeso, scala indigeat, quem Pater inter manus bajulat, ut ad tertii coeli secreta rapiat, intantum ut glorietur, et dicat: *Dextera tua suscepit me. Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me, et cum gloria suscepisti me? [n: (Psal. XVII.)]* Non ergo opus hic habet Spiritus [1115A] ille de medio sublatus officio scalae, nec eget in illa subtilitatis suae ascensione sustentari alicujus corporeae similitudinis adumbratione, ubi videt facie ad faciem, non per speculum, et in aenigmate. Mentior si ipsi de seipsis non idem asserunt qui ejusmodi sunt: *Nos autem omnes,* inquiunt, *revelata facie, gloriam Domini speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu [n: (II Cor. III)]*. Vides certe quid agat, et intelligis, ut arbitror, quid valeat illa divisio animae et spiritus, de qua superius jam diximus. Spiritus ab infimis dividitur ut ad summa sublimetur. Spiritus ab anima scinditur ut Domino uniatur. Qui enim adhaeret Domino, unus spiritus est. Felix divisio, et exspectabilis separatio, ubi quod [1115B] passibile, quod corruptibile dignoscitur, suis interim passionibus moritur, usque adeo ut nihil passibilitatis, nihil corruptibilitatis interim sentiatur; ubi et illud quod spirituale, quod subtile, usque ad speculationem divinae gloriae sublimatur, et in eamdem imaginem transformatur. Pars igitur inferior componitur ad summam pacem et tranquillitatem, pars autem superior sublimatur ad gloriam et jucunditatem. Sic faciem Moysi (superiorem sane corporis partem) a consortio Domini glorificatam agnovimus, ita ut non possent filii Israel intendere vultum ejus propter claritatem ipsius. Quis, quaeso, digne dicere, quis explicare sufficiat quid perfectionis in excessus sui glorificatione spiritus acquirat, [1115C] quamvis peregrinationis suae protelationem usque in diem tertium non extendat, etiamsi silentii moram usque ad dimidiam horam non producat, [1116A] licet eat et redeat in similitudinem fulguris coruscantis? Sic Moyses de consortio divini colloquii, cum clarificato vultu etiam cornua reportat, ostendens quid virtutis, quid fortitudinis de ejus contubernio contraxerit, qui dat virtutem et fortitudinem plebi suae benedictus Deus. Redit ergo tandem, et revertitur ad se spiritus ille qui longe excesserat supra se, et quod passibile et corruptibile posuerat, quasi impassibile et incorruptibile ad prioris status comparationem resumit, et in novitatem vitae resurgit. Quid tibi videtur ad illatam injuriam hilarescere, ad objectam contumeliam non erubescere, de tribulatione gaudere? nonne hoc est in novitate vitae ambulare, et secundum aliquem modum seipsum impassibilem ostendere, et suis passionibus [1116B] non subjacere? Ecce quousque proficiunt qui in hoc lapide requiescunt. Multa sunt quae de hac materia dici potuissent, si hoc loco dici debuissent et moderatae digressionis mensuram non excederent. Puto enim hoc novissimum genus lapidum omnium esse dignissimum atque pretiosissimum. Nullum tamen debemus spernere, sed singulos saltem de singulis quaerere, et in unum congregare.

Notandum sane hoc esse primum opus, quod in terra promissionis fieri praecipitur, ut divinorum operum aeternum memoriale primo omnium constituatur. Sine hoc enim lapidum cumulo, Dominica illa aeternae haereditatis promissio nunquam fortiter acquiritur, nunquam secure possidetur. Qui enim beneficiorum [1116C] divinitus perceptorum obliviscitur, ad majora obtinenda promoveri non meretur.

## THE FIRST TREATISE.



## CHAPTER ONE.

[1073C]

*What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled; and thou, O Jordan, that thou art turned back? [n: (Psal. CXIII.)]* This utterance of the Prophet is an exclamation, with wonder; and the wonder is with exultation. For he was seeing a certain divine miracle; and not one only, but a twofold one, each great, each wondrous, each exceedingly astounding. He saw the sea flee before the face of Israel; he saw the Jordan bend the rush of its course back toward its spring; he saw both give way to the Hebrew people and leave a free road to those setting out. Which of these is not new, which of these is not wondrous? He contemplated each thus, and marvelled at each, and rejoiced over each. He cries out, therefore, in the voice of exultation and of confession: [1073D] What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled: and thou, O Jordan, that thou art turned back? The first miracle happens at Israel's going out from Egypt, but the second happens at Israel's going out from the desert. Who at length will one day grant me perfectly to forsake the region of unlikeness: who could grant me to enter into the land of promise, so that I might be able to see alike the flight of the sea and the turning back of the Jordan? A fair spectacle it is, and pleasant enough, to see the water of the sea fleeing, to see the water of the Jordan returning, the bitter withdraw, the sweet flow back, bitterness fail, sweetness [1074C] overflow. Whoever thou art that seest these things, I should wonder if thou too didst not cry out: *What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled; and thou, O Jordan, that thou art turned back?* Miracles of this kind are never wont to happen except before true Jews, except before good Hebrews.

## CHAPTER II. *On the twofold confession, and the twofold advancement.*

Confession makes the Jew, passage makes the Hebrew. For "Jew" is interpreted *confessing,* "Hebrew" *passing over.* And there is a true confession, and there is a feigned confession. Likewise there is a good passage and there is a bad passage. True confession makes a true Jew, and a good passage makes a good Hebrew. To ascribe to thyself thy evils, to ascribe to thy God thy goods — that is true confession, right confession. The former is of crime, the latter of praise; each of them indeed [1074D] useful, each praiseworthy. Likewise the passage is double; each of them indeed good, each necessary. He who passes from evil to good passes well indeed; and he who passes from good to best, he too makes a good passage. Know, therefore, and confess thy evils, and do not remain in them; but pass beyond them, and the first passage is made, and the first confession. Likewise confess to God concerning thy goods, praise him for his goods, and do not grow sluggish in them: but strive as much as thou canst toward better things, and pass over to the best, and the second passage is made, and the second confession. [1075A] At the first confession the first miracle is wont to happen, and at the second confession the second miracle is wont to happen. For through the confession of crime the flight of the sea is brought about, and at the confession of praise the Jordan is straightway turned back.

## CHAPTER III. *How the confession of crime avails for the extermination of evil.*

For all things are washed in confession: the conscience is cleansed, bitterness is taken away, the sea is put to flight, tranquillity returns, hope revives, in spirits it grows glad. For blessed are they that mourn, since they shall be comforted. What is it to mourn, to be made sorrowful, but to be driven by the storms of the sea? And what is the joy of consolation but the flight of the sea and the absenting of grief? Hear [1075B] the Jew confessing his crimes, and mark the water of the sea fleeing before him: *I said,* he says, *I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my sin [n: (Psal. XXXI)]*. He was confessing his iniquity, and the sea was being put to flight, because his impiety was being forgiven. For impiety is a sea, since it cannot make sweet water; but its water is exceedingly salt and very bitter, and its bitterness is a most bitter bitterness. What sweetness, I ask, has envy? What sweet taste, I beseech thee, has wrath; what pleasantness has impatience? Waters of this kind, as I judge, are every one of them bitter, and they make a sea, because they can taste good to none at all, can please no one. Dost thou see, then, what manner of thing this great sea is, and wide of hands, which can [1075C] be called the sea of malice. For there is also another which can be called the sea of misery, having indeed itself water by no means sweet, yet less bitter. But happy is he who has dominion from sea to sea, so that he lies under no fault, succumbs to no penalty, to such a degree that all iniquity may not have dominion over him, nor any adversity oppress him. Happy the man before whose face the sea flees malice withdraws, misery gives way, the conscience grows glad. Can it be that one who is such is unable to sing confidently? What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled? If therefore thou also wilt, make of thyself a Jew of good profession; confess from thy heart thy sin, that thou too mayest be able to see such a spectacle, so great a miracle, and mayest not hesitate to sing a hymn of this kind. [1075D] What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled?

## CHAPTER IV. *How the confession of praise avails for the advancement of good.*

But now let us consider this, how at the confession of praise the turning back of the Jordan is wont to happen. But this, as I judge, we learn better by working than by disputing; this we prove more quickly by experiencing than by speaking. In short, do thou also busy thyself to confess, to marvel at, to venerate God's power, God's wisdom, God's mercy; and be assured that the more thou shalt praise, the more ardently shalt thou love. Let it not irk thee, then, to praise the divine grace much, that thou mayest love much; to love much, that thou mayest desire much. For the more vehemently thou shalt desire, the more quickly wilt thou obtain [1076A] what thou greatly covetest. Love what before thou didst despise, despise what before thou didst love, and be secure, for the Jordan is turned back. Love God, scorn the world, and I will truly acknowledge that the Jordan is turned back. What manner of turning back of the Jordan is this, I ask: how wonderful, how praiseworthy, how lovable — that the whole rush of love, the whole inundation of love, the whole affluence of delight should run with great haste not downward but upward, should seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth; so that thou mayest truly profess that the Jordan is turned back! This, as I judge, was the reason why it neither irked the Prophet nor shamed him to become a Jew: because he had truly acknowledged that *It is good to confess to the Lord, and [1076B] to sing to thy name, O Most High [n: (Psal. XCI)]*. Hence that firm profession and devout promise: *I will confess to the Lord exceedingly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him [n: (Psal. CVIII)]*. Did he not will himself to be a Jew, when he said: *Praise the Lord, O my soul? [n: (Psal. CXLV.)]* Did he not forbid the water of the Jordan to flow downward, when he admonished his own soul with a coaxing address? *Hope in God, for I will still confess to him, the salvation of my countenance, and my God [n: (Psal. XLII)]*. Did he not desire the streams of the Jordan to be turned back, when he said: *Turn, O my soul, into thy rest, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee [n: (Psal. CXIV)]*. I should wonder if thou wilt hear this and not thyself seek to become a Jew, and to confess to the Lord, since he is good, since his mercy endureth unto the age, and to be found worthy — one to whom the Lord may deign [1076C] to show so great a miracle, that thou mayest sing with the Prophet: for the Jordan is turned back.

## CHAPTER V. *That the first advancement of virtue lies in contempt of the world.*

But let not even that, I ask, be enough for thee, when thou hast become a Jew, unless thou be made likewise a Hebrew also. Assuredly the Hebrews themselves are the very same as the Jews, although Jews on one account and Hebrews on another. For confession, as has been said, makes the Jew, and passage makes the Hebrew. In short, do thou thyself also, if thou art in Egypt, pass over and forsake Egypt, and thou hast made a Hebrew of good hope, and thou wilt see in the flight of the sea that great and astounding miracle. But if thou shalt take pains to pass over the desert itself as well, thou wilt see things yet greater [1076D] than these in the turning back of the Jordan. The first passage, then, is out of Egypt, the second out of the desert. First pass from the world to thyself, second from thyself into God, Thou hast loved the world, scorn the world, and pass over. Forsake the cares of this world, and take care of thyself, and thou beginnest to be a dweller of the wilderness. Returning from the darkness of Egypt, from worldly errors, to the more secret places of the heart, thou wilt find nothing else but a place of horror and of vast solitude. For this is that land desert, pathless, and waterless — the conscience, namely, long neglected, wholly untilled, beset with thorns and thistles, and full of every horror. Thou must therefore forsake Egypt and seek a wilderness of this kind, if thou desirest to behold with thine own eyes the flight of the sea, as David also went far off in flight and abode in the solitude; fulfil, [1077A] O transgressor, what is enjoined upon transgressors, where it is said: *Return, ye transgressors, to the heart [n: (Isai. XLVI)]*, and the first passage is made, and henceforth thou art rightly called a Hebrew.



## CHAPTER VI. *That the second advancement of virtue lies in contempt of self.*

Return, therefore, to thyself, and with all keeping keep thy heart. But woe to thee if thou remainest there. Do not remain, but pass over, going on, and passing through into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. Pass over, then, thyself also; go on into thy God; seek and lay hold of the highest good. Hear her who cries aloud in the streets; hearken to the voice of Wisdom, admonishing us to this second passage: *Pass over to me,* she says, *all ye that covet me (Eccle. [1077B] XXIV)*. Forsake the world, and Israel's passage out of Egypt is made. Despise thyself, and Israel's passage out of the desert is made. The first passage, then, contempt of the world makes; the second passage contempt of self brings about. At the first passage the sea is put to flight. At the second passage the Jordan is turned back. The flight of the sea is the extermination of bitterness. The turning back of the Jordan is the reordering of charity.

## CHAPTER VII. *How through contempt of the world the extermination of evil comes about.*

Wouldst thou hear more openly, know more fully how at the first passage of the Hebrews, in what manner at contempt of the world, the flight of the sea, the extermination of bitterness, comes about. [1077C] Straightway and without doubt, as soon as thou hast forsaken Egypt, as soon as thou hast cast the whole world behind thee: the cause of fear perishes, the cause of grief, the root of bitterness (for cupidity is the root of all evils). For when thou shalt be able fully to escape the world, when thou shalt have begun to covet none of its prosperities, to dread none of its adversities, what will there then be that could disturb thy mind? What, I ask, do we more rightly understand by the flight of the sea than to be wearied by no perturbations? In short, let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid, and the sea, fleeing before our face, has gone away and withdrawn. I think that the sea will be no more when God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, when there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any grief at all, since [1077D] the former things are passed away. For what are fear and trembling and sorrow, but waters of the sea exceedingly bitter, and wholly devoid of all sweetness? The Prophet came into the depth of a sea of this kind, unless I am mistaken, when he said: *Fear and trembling came upon me [n: (Psal. LIV)]*. And that other word: *Tribulation and anguish have found me [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. A sea of this kind they meet with, as many as forsake Egypt, seek the desert, covet the land of promise. For we must pass through many tribulations into the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER VIII. *That contrition of spirit is now for a help, now for the support of good.*

A sea of this kind some have before them, but others behind them. Those, however, who have it before them — to them it is for a hindrance; [1078A] those who have it beside them, to them it is for a help; those who have it behind them, to them it is for a support. And so the Israelites, forsaking Egypt, wishing to enter the desert, and sighing after the land of promise, first had the sea before them for a hindrance to their setting out; afterward they had it beside them for a help of defense, when it was to them for a wall on the right hand and on the left; at last they had it behind them for a support of security, their enemies having been drowned or shut off by it. Before us are things to come, beside us things present, behind us things past. The sea before us is the fear of dangers to come. The sea beside us is the labor of the conflicts pressing upon us. The sea behind us is the grief of evils committed; the sea before us, the fear of faint-heartedness; the sea beside us, the labor [1078B] of solicitude; the sea behind us, the grief of repentance. The fear of faint-heartedness hinders; the labor of solicitude fortifies; the grief of repentance protects. One man, considering the life and the zeal of others, when he sees many — even after the vow of profession — return to their vomit and go back to the world, does not so much as dare to begin what is good: this man has the sea before him, but for a hindrance. For what is the trembling of the heart, the hesitation of the mind, but a kind of billowing, as it were, of the sea? For he who has hesitated is like a wave of the sea, which is moved and carried about by the wind. Another manfully tramples this fear, puts the billowings of the sea to flight before him, chastises the trembling of his heart, bravely prepares his spirit to endure whatever perils for the Lord, and for this part does not hesitate to sing, the sea saw [1078C] and fled — inasmuch as all useless trembling flees and departs before his face. But because he is still solicitous how he ought either to beware of negligence in good things or to avoid the stealthy approach of evils, he does indeed suffer the sea, though not before him, yet on either side, inasmuch as he must act constantly on this hand toward good things, on that hand against evils, must labor much, and be solicitous on both sides. But happy are those whom now the exercises of the virtues, the conflicts of labors, do not so much weary as delight — who, though they lament only this, that they have consumed so many seasons of their past life either in iniquity, or squandered them in vanity. He who is of this kind shows that he has the sea behind his back, like him who said: *I will recount [1078D] to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul [n: (Isa. XXXVIII)]*. But who would doubt that for men of this kind the sea has been left behind their back, for a most safe support, and for the overthrow of their enemies? For the bitterness of penitence is wont not only to blot out by satisfaction the evils committed, but it has also been accustomed to bring this about in us: that what is not lawful should not even please us to repeat.

## CHAPTER IX. *On useful and useless contrition.*

Let us consider this also: how here the water of the sea, the wave of bitterness, is to some outside the way, to others in the way. Who would doubt that this life is the way to the life to come? One man grieves for those things which belong to the present life, another for those which belong to the life to come. He who grieves for those things [1079A] which are in this life, to him the sea is in the way. He who grieves for those which are outside this life, to him the sea is beside the way. In this life, both goods and evils; in that life, either goods alone, or evils alone. And so the things which are nothing differ much from one another, and touch one another by no nearness of likeness, inasmuch as between them a great chasm has been fixed, in which no proportion of a like quality can be found. But this life lies as it were midway between those things which belong to the life to come, the goods but the evils, inasmuch as it approaches both, on this side or on that, by some likeness, since it has goods and evils mingled together. Therefore with the goods of that life, by the goods of its own (although it is joined by a shadowy likeness, as also with the evils of that life, by the evils of its own), it is allied by an imaginary affinity. Outside, therefore, [1079B] this way are those things which come after this life. Outside indeed, and beside — not only by likeness of quality, but by the cohesion of time. As soon as we forsake these, we fall into those without delay. He therefore who fears, grieves and laments for these things, pours out the wave of sorrow, the affluence of bitterness, like the water of the sea, beside the way of its own running down.

## CHAPTER X. *On the twofold compunction of the heart.*

Sorrow for us eternal ones is the sea on the right hand; sorrow for eternal evils is the sea on the left hand. Assuredly, if we are of sound mind, for both we ought to to fear [sic: *time re*], to grieve, and to abound in the bitter tears of compunction. Let us fear to lose these, let us fear to incur those, [1079C] and we have a twofold sea strongly fortifying us, and that on either side. Rightly, as I judge, the sea which meets us in the way, which hinders the journey of our setting out, which blocks the course of our progress, we strike with the rod of just severity, we terrify by consideration of the divine strictness, we remove by remembrance of the examination to come. Let all our dread, then, all our sorrow be removed from the way; and, for a useless life, for the solicitude of worldly life, let our compunction be divided into two, that by the sorrow of fear we may wash away eternal evils, and by the tears of desire may purchase eternal goods. Happy are they who pass through this twofold sea also of a double sorrow, who leave far behind their back every ambiguity and dread of what is to be expected in time to come, and pass over the whole mourning of diffidence [1079D] by the security of sure hope — would that in us too a dread and sorrow of this kind might be swallowed up by the security of a confidence coming upon us! Let a sea of this kind also flee and depart, that we too may be able to sing with the Prophet: What ails thee, O sea, that thou hast fled? Do we not think the sea from beside, that one had fled away, who was saying? *I have fought the good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: for the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the just judge shall render to me in that day [n: (II Tim. IV)]*. I think that he had left every sea far behind his back, nor was there anything whence he then ought to have been made sorrowful and troubled, when he was saying: I am conscious to myself of nothing.



## CHAPTER XI. *On the vain or the true contempt of the world*

But what, I ask, do we say that this is: that even [1080A] today we see so many forsake Egypt who nevertheless do not deserve to behold so great a miracle in the flight of the sea? If they truly forsake Egypt, if they are true Hebrews, inasmuch as they pass over out of the world and make the first passage of the Hebrews, why do they not take experience at least of the first miracle also? Or do they perhaps leave the world by profession, but not also by manner of life — in habit, not in affection? If it behooves me to glory, I can glory for this part only. If indeed they are Hebrews, so am I. But see lest perchance it be not enough for us and for you to have changed place, not spirit: they change the world, not the spirit, who run across the sea. What good is it thus to pass over and not to make a Hebrew? Without doubt, at Israel's going out from Egypt, the flight of the sea shows how rightly each man claims for himself the dignity of this [1080B] name.

## CHAPTER XII. *How difficult it is to attain to perfect contempt of self.*

Let us pass out of Egypt in body; let us pass out also in heart. But let us not think that this can suffice us either. For a great way still remains for us, if we wish to attain to the vision of the second miracle. Far beyond doubt, it is not a matter of the same capacity, or of the same ease, to go out of Egypt and to pass through the wilderness, to leave the world and to conquer oneself and to cast oneself behind. The former is as it were a small thing, which is accomplished in a small time; the latter, after many labors, through many temptations, is scarcely at length and by few ever completed. The former is the work of a single day; the latter we scarcely fulfil after many [1080C] seasons. Hard, difficult, great it is to leave oneself, to look well into oneself and fully to scorn oneself, to approve by the perfect and utterly to disapprove. Here is the labor, here the groaning. Depraved is the heart of man and unsearchable, and who shall know it? Ye sons of men, how long will ye be heavy of heart, with stiff neck and untameable heart — and who shall conquer it?

## CHAPTER XIII. *By what means the mind is trained to full contempt of self.*

O how often it is necessary to change places, how often to pitch camp, how many temptations to endure, to prove all things, to hold what is good, to abstain from every evil appearance! O how often it is necessary to go and to return, and to forget the things that are [1080D] behind, and to stretch forward to the things before, and again, by going back behind one's own back, to take experience of oneself, and through one's own failing to be taught one's own infirmity! O how often it is necessary to fall into so many bypaths of errors, so many shadowed places of ambiguities, so many monsters of vices — to traverse them, to look upon them — before one hold the far bounds of the wilderness, and come to the uttermost of humility, and perfectly attain to the highest contempt of self! O how often it is necessary to flee to God's mercy, and, caught amid so many perils, to seek the divine mercy and to obtain grace! O how astounding the mighty works! O how delightful the miracles! O how wonderful the benefits which — in so many divine revelations, in such visitations, in such consolations — they experience, marvel at, venerate, whom [1081A] the vastness of the wilderness and the greatness of their own infirmity have taught to trust nothing of their own virtue, but to presume the whole of it from God's mercy, to cast their care upon the Lord, and to place their hope in the Lord God! There it is granted to experience, in the sweetness of the heavenly food, how great is the multitude of sweetness which God has hidden for them that love him; to taste and see how pleasant the Lord is, and how good the God of Israel is to them that are right of heart. There they who ascend into the mountain of the Lord and draw near to his feet shall receive of his doctrine, proving and professing that great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number. And so whoever, in that land desert and waterless, has known this — thus he appeared to him in the sanctuary, that he might see his power and his glory — taking experience of that saying, [1081B] that great is the Lord, and exceedingly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end. But who could enumerate how innumerable are the alternating vicissitudes of this kind — now of desolations, now of consolations — that must be experienced; how many judgments of human infirmity, how many proofs of the divine mercy it falls to the dwellers of the wilderness and the worshippers of God to see, before they reach the far bounds of the wilderness and lay hold of the bounds of perfect humility; before the wave of the Jordan give way to those who come and, turning back its course, return to its spring; and the human spirit, spurning its own things and despising itself, pass over wholly into God, and run by desire into him from whom is every best gift and every perfect boon, and turn back to [1081C] God, the living fountain, the whole rush of its love.

## CHAPTER XIV *That superfluous love of self is more hardly overcome amid the successes of the virtues.*

O happy soul, thou who art worthy — thou for whom the Lord deigns to work so great a miracle, to whom it is granted to see such a spectacle: the waters which are lower, and whatever streams of desires tend toward the depths, running down and failing, and the waters which come from above, the desires which are from on high, standing together in a single mass — so that she may truly sing: *One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life [n: (Psal. XXVI)]*. O unhappy soul, thou who delayest, who dost not hasten, who dost not greatly [1081D] pant to run and to see, to marvel and to be astounded that the streams of the Jordan first fix their course, stand in one place, and cling immovably in one desire of eternity, and thereafter utterly fail in the lower parts and little by little increase in the higher. What miracle, I beseech thee, dost thou think it, what prodigy, that the Jordan should be driven backward, and so great a rush of the river return to the upper parts — especially if it happen at the time of harvest, when it is wont to fill the banks of its channel? For when that seed which fell upon the good ground has begun to bring forth fruit of itself, one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold, then indeed the wave of the Jordan is wont to swell higher; and, as is the way of the human spirit, to esteem great things of itself, to believe itself someone great, when it has seen itself bring forth much fruit and [1082A] come to the harvest of ripeness. Then — no wonder — the greater the things it esteems of itself, by so much the greater love does it judge itself worthy of; and it is a very great thing if it does not flow out even unto the depths of superfluity, and does not overpass the bounds of just equity and the banks of usefulness. How great, then, dost thou think, how great a miracle dost thou reckon it, to grow cheap to thyself, to displease thyself more and more, and that especially at the time when thou beginnest truly to be great and to appear great to all? The waters of the Jordan are indeed wont — nor is this a wonder — at the time of icy cold, or even by the drought of summer heat, to be lessened and to shrink; and any mind, however exalted, amid the cold of malice and the excessive heats of concupiscence, to grow cheap to itself, and, however unwillingly, to acknowledge its own infirmity, and to subside not a little from its own estimation [1082B] of itself. Who, I ask, is so monstrously foolish as not sometimes to displease himself amid wickednesses and outrages? But this will be the great thing: if at the time of harvest, and amid the successes of the virtues, he can shut in the waves of the Jordan within the banks of its channel, and restrain the rush of private love within the bounds of modesty. It will be a great thing if it does not burst out to unlawful things, or flow away to useless ones. It will be a great thing if he does not even love himself except so far as is fitting, or expedient. *But the Jordan,* says the Scripture, *had filled the banks of its channel at the time of harvest [n: (Josue VIII)]*. It had filled, it says, not overpassed. It will not be harmful, then, as I think, to fill the banks, but to overpass the banks.



## CHAPTER XV. *How the spirit is to be advanced step by step to contempt of self.*

[1082C]

The first thing, then, for each man is to restrain love of self to a fixed measure, that afterward he may deserve to see that great and astounding miracle also: the Jordan, namely, first indeed fixing its course, then swelling, at last going backward and ascending to the higher places. And that first thing indeed — namely, to check excess — although great, is nevertheless not wondrous; but to bend the course back toward the mountains is a wonderful spectacle and a spectacular miracle. Altogether and beyond doubt it is one thing to temper love of self, and another to hold it back and turn it aside. Moderated love of self is one thing, and great contempt of self another. I think it was not without cause that such a miracle was celebrated nowhere but in the Jordan, [1082D] which is interpreted *their descent.* But what is that descent but the humbling of the heart? Or of whom is it "their," unless of those very ones who descend and humble themselves willingly? For those whose descent is not voluntary — it is indeed in them, but in a certain way it is not theirs, because it does not profit them. It must therefore be of their own accord, that it may profit them and may truly be called theirs. Are they thought [sic: *ereduntur*] to have descended of their own accord, or to have profited anything in this, of whom it is read: *Thou hast cast them down while they were lifted up? [n: (Psal. LXXXVIII.)]* He therefore who wishes to see that great miracle must descend from every elation of mind and be humbled by a willing will — not like those who were cast down unwillingly, to the praise of God indeed, though to no profit of their own. So then, only in the Jordan, in the descent [1083A] of them, in the descent of those who descend, in the humbling of those who humble themselves, is so renowned a deed and heavenly miracle wrought. The greater thou art, therefore, humble thyself in all things, and thou keepest the banks of the Jordan: worthy that the Jordan give way to thee, that the Lord show thee miracles.

## CHAPTER XVI. *How, when vain love has been drained away, the spirit is enlarged in the love of God.*

Wouldst thou see the waters of the Jordan fix their course and stand in one place? *But for me,* he says, *it is good to cleave to God; to put my hope in the Lord God [n: (Psal. LXXXII)]*. Wouldst thou see the lower waters run down and fail? *My soul refused to be comforted [n: (Psal. LXXXVI)]*. Wouldst thou see the upper waters swell and run upward? *As the hart longeth after the fountains [1083B] of waters, so longeth my soul after thee, O God [n: (Psal. XLI)]*. In short, do thou also not go after thy concupiscences, and thou hast fixed the waters. Love not the world, nor the things that are in the world: and the lower waters, which run downward, have failed. In short, delight thou in the Lord, and thou wilt see them stand fixed in one place. Love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind, and thou wilt see the waters swell vehemently and rise up — nor is it a wonder — into a great mass. I think thou canst find nothing whereby to spread them more widely than to pour them out with the whole heart, and to stretch them through the whole soul, and out of them to fill the whole mind. O how vehemently this saving wave had swelled in the breast of him who said: *I desire to be dissolved, [1083C] and to be with Christ! [n: (Philipp. VIII.)]* To this same sense runs that which the Prophet, in singing, declared of himself: *My soul hath fainted after thy salvation [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. But what manner of inundation of waters, I ask, was that, where a father is compelled to cry out for a parricide son? *Absalom my son, my son Absalom: who would grant me that I might die for thee, Absalom my son? [n: (II Reg. XXIX.)]* I think no place could be found whither they might spread themselves more widely. For no one has greater charity than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. So too that inundation swelled not a little, concerning which we have the Lord's own testimony: *Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much [n: (Luc. VII)]*. What wonder, I ask, if those things appeared from afar which had swelled much? Do you wish to know how far off appears [1083D] the inundation of that love which surged so greatly, which bowed itself even to the kissing and the anointing of the feet: *Amen I say to you, wheresoever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done shall be told in memory of her [n: (Matth. XXVI)]*. But do you wish to know yet more openly how far off they can appear, if only they have swelled after the fashion of a mountain? *In this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one toward another [n: (Joan. XIII)]*. How far off, I beseech thee, does that appear which all men must know? But it is necessary, as we have already said, that the streams of true charity swell after the fashion of a mountain, if they would appear so far off. But perhaps thou art still seeking the mountain, after whose likeness thou readest that the waters swelled. See whether perhaps it be that curdled mountain, [1084A] the fat mountain, the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared on the top of the mountains — inasmuch as the Lord has exalted him and given him a name which is above every name, that in the name of Jesus every thing may bend the knee, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. After the fashion of this mountain, after the likeness of that great and wonderful love by which he laid down his life for his sheep, let him know that the waters must swell who desires them to appear from afar and to fulfil the Lord's precept: *This is my precept, that you love one another, as I have loved you [n: (ibid.)]*. Hear the likeness, and apply imitation. As I have loved you, he says. The likeness of love is after the fashion of a mountain. How much did he love us, who died for our sake? Can it be that they did not hold the likeness of this mountain in their love [1084B] — they who for Christ were stoned, were cut asunder, were tempted, died in the slaying of the sword? For this reason, as I judge, their sound went out into all the earth and their words unto the ends of the world: that they might appear from afar, that they might be seen by all, and that all might imitate them. But why, I ask, do we wonder if those waters appeared from afar which, as it is written: *swelled even unto Sartan? [n: (Josue III.)]* Sartan is interpreted *their tribulation.* But what else is their tribulation, according to what we have already said concerning the Jordan, but the tribulation of the tribulated? And a voluntary tribulation is each man's own. For what each man takes up patiently, or even gladly, he makes his own, because he compels it to serve his own profit. As therefore the descent is the descent of those who willingly [1084C] humble themselves, so also the tribulation is the tribulation of those who for the Lord's sake love tribulation. And so that tribulation is the tribulation of the tribulated which is reckoned to the tribulated for merit. See, then, those waters which were the upper ones — how much they had grown, how much they had swelled, which had stretched themselves even unto Sartan. O love, strong as death, thou who dost stretch thyself even unto Sartan, and dost spread thy bosom even unto voluntary tribulation? What manner of enlargement of love, I ask, is this; what manner of inundation of waters — to stretch and enlarge one's own heart even unto voluntary tribulation, unto willing suffering, unto a death that is wished for? Doubt not, then, that the upper waters have stretched themselves to that place, as often as thou seest men rejoicing in tribulation [1084D] and loving their own tribulation for the Lord's sake, as the apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were held worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus.



## CHAPTER XVII. *On the failing of vain love, and the progress of true love.*

Therefore the upper waters ascend even unto Sartan, and the lower waters descend even unto the sea. The former ascend and grow, the latter descend and diminish. The former grow and swell, the latter diminish and fail. A fair spectacle, that the upper waters swell about Sartan and the lower waters fail in the sea. Here give heed and be astounded. Here give heed diligently, and be astounded vehemently. Choose, among things so great and so much to be wondered at, what [1085A] thou shouldst wonder at first, what thou shouldst wonder at more: whether that waters among the mountains do not flow down but swell, or that waters out of waters do not swell but fail. *But the waters,* says the Scripture, *which were the lower ones went down into the sea of solitude, which is now called the Dead, until they wholly failed [n: (Josue III)]*. Those, then, which are lower must needs descend into the sea and fail in the sea. But we know that, however sweet the waters may be, since, when they come into the sea, they cannot keep their own sweetness. Those, then, which descend into the sea quickly grow bitter. *Let your laughter,* he says, *be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow [n: (Jac. IV)]* — that is, for sweet water to descend into the sea, and to lose its sweetness, and to turn the sweet into the bitter. Laughter indeed and joy make sweet [1085B] water, and of this kind, howsoever ardently each man thirsts, so gladly also does he drink. But mourning and sorrow cannot make water sweet, nor do men readily wish to drink of this kind. As often as laughter is turned into mourning, so often does the lower water slip into the sea and be changed into bitter. For that laughter cannot belong to the upper waters of which it was said by the mouth of Truth: Woe to you that now laugh, for you shall weep. What, then, is it for the lower waters to run down into the sea and to fail, but to draw carnal and lowest delights into grief, and to extinguish them by repenting? For he who laments and groans over a delight already committed, who shudders at one coming upon him and spits it out, who fears one to come and busies himself to avoid it — what else does he do than turn the sweet into the bitter for himself? This, then, this, [1085C] I say, is what we were wondering at above, what we wonder at still: to turn the sweet into the bitter, to bewail joy, to grieve over delight, and in this manner for the sweet to fail in the sea. Do the waters, then, swell about Sartan; do the waters, then, fail in the sea? Is it thus, O man, that thou rejoicest over tribulation? Is it thus, O man, that thou art troubled over delight? O wondrous, O astounding! In voluntary tribulation joys are heaped up; the delights that come to meet us are exterminated by a grief freely taken.

## CHAPTER XVIII. *How, through the failing of vain love, the perturbations of the mind fail.*

But what, I ask, does this mean, that it is called [1085D] the Dead Sea, in which so renowned a deed came to pass? Why, I ask, did it receive such a name? For that it did not have it before, the Scripture sufficiently intimates in this, that it says: *The sea of solitude, which is now called the Dead (Josue III)*. I think that not every sea of solitude, nor every bitterness of desolation — nay, this very sea of which we are now speaking — is by no means worthily reckoned by such a name; nor ought it be called dead, unless perchance the aforesaid miracle come to pass in it. We know that what is dead cannot move itself at all; perhaps this sea, after the wave falling into it had failed, after it no longer had a flood flowing in and driving it, fell away from its own seething, and lost those swelling and boiling storms of its own billowings. For the inflowing rushes of the Jordan, and its most rapid course, [1086A] by their most vehement gliding-in used to drive it and shake it, and did not at all suffer it to be tranquil and quiet.
