In this stone he bravely endured the blows of the stones that pressed upon him, and he feared neither the hands of them that stoned him nor the onset of them that gnashed with their teeth at him [n: (Act. VII)]. O stone strong and hard, yet full of sweetness! O breast most robust, yet full of mercy! You wonder, whoever you are that hear, how in his patience he possessed his soul; but you ought rather to have wondered how his mind, under so great a bitterness of persecution, did not lose its own sweetness. By his enemies he was pressed, and for his enemies he prayed. He was enduring human savagery, and [1110B] he was looking up to the divine glory: *Behold,* he says, *I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God [n: (ibid.)]*. On earth he was pressed, and from the heavens he was consoled. He was afflicted by the misery brought upon him, he was moved by the mercy grown within him, he rejoiced at the glory beheld. Behold, at one and the same time he saw below that whereat he might have compassion, he saw above that whereat he might be glad. Behold how from the same breast there flowed mercy with gladness, gladness with mercy. Behold how from the same vessel there flows oil with honey, the oil of mercy with the honey of gladness. What, I ask, is this unmingled confusion and unconfused commingling of oil and honey in that stone? I marvel if you do not marvel how that strong fighter at one and the same moment sucked honey out of the rock and oil out of the hardest crag. [1110C] Marvellous is the virtue of patience; and who may worthily weigh the price of this rock, which in so great abundance distils oil with honey? How great an abundance of oil and of honey, I ask, is found to be within, where mercy is diminished by no malice, where sweetness is thinned by no grief? Nay, in a wondrous manner delight grows out of grief, and compassion out of suffering. The martyr indeed, when he was being stoned, had more pity upon his enemies than upon his own limbs. For kneeling down he prayed, saying: *Lord, lay not this sin to their charge, for they know not what they do [n: (ibid.)]*. Behold, at the placing of his knees the oil was poured out, and thereafter his name was made as oil poured out. For at the pitying of his enemy the pouring out of the oil was made, so much so that [1110D] the young man who sat at a distance was sprinkled with the odor of the ointment. For when the body was bowed and the head bent down, the oil began to flow forth, and it was made as ointment upon the head, and it ran down to the hem of the garment of him who kept the garments. Rising up therefore swiftly, he who had long sat in dark places and in the shadow of death began to run after the odor of the ointments; and exulting as a giant to run his way, whithersoever was the onset of the Spirit, thither he went, and thereafter he became the good odor of Christ in every place.

## CHAPTER XV. *On the solicitude of circumspection.*

The ninth rock I find in Hezekiah; I find it also in the friend's bride and the bridegroom's friend, to whom [1111A] it is said in the Canticles: *Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall [n: (Cant. II)]*. So too Hezekiah, after the likeness of the bride choosing quiet and seeking after solitude, and sitting in the clefts of the rock, or even in the hollow of the wall, cried out thus as the young of a swallow, and meditated as a dove: Oh who will give me wings like a dove's, and I will fly away and be at rest, if perchance I may be able to fly forth into that place where the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may lay her young! Where, I ask, will anything of safety be found, if it be not found in the clefts of a rock of this kind, where zealous premeditation foresees whatever dangers before they come to pass, and, forestalling the things to come, gathers the future out of the past, and often knows beforehand the undoubted [1111B] outcomes of doubtful matters? For what else is circumspection, but the solicitous and sagacious searching out of the evils that stand round about? To this belongs the going back over past evils, the consideration of present ones, the premeditation of those to come, so that according to its own name it may truly be circumspection. The assiduity of this makes a man cautious, and, so far as is possible, renders him safe.

## CHAPTER XVI. *On the assiduity of speculation.*

The tenth stone has been called the assiduity of speculation. Jacob, turning away from evil and giving place to wrath, while he sets out abroad in haste, lest his flight should be in the winter or on the Sabbath, found this stone upon the road, [1111C] and having found it placed it under his head, lest he should not have where to lay his head while he slept upon the way [n: (Gen. XXVIII)]. Upon this stone, in peace, in the selfsame he sleeps and rests, and upon the road he found that rest which they cannot find even in chambers and on purple couches who are clothed in soft garments and are in the houses of kings. And so, Jacob's head being laid down upon this stone, and the eyes of concupiscence being closed (which we read were open in our first parent), while upon this headrest he is lulled in deep quiet, while he gladly forgets all outward things, his mind wakes up to inward things, and sees what before, while waking and seeing, it could not see. A ladder reaching up to heaven is raised before his eyes, and the Lord is seen leaning upon the ladder, so that through invisible form and the figure of invisible things [1111D] the mind of the beholder may be lifted up into the understanding of intelligible things. Happy the man for whom the knowledge of visible things becomes a ladder for knowing invisible things. A beautiful spectacle it is to see the rungs of this ladder set in fitting manner and in due proportion, and carried up to the topmost point by the continuity of an ordered distinction, so that through the manifold difference of creatures and the gradation of dignities, ordinately distinguished and distinctly ordered, the mind may little by little advance itself to higher things, and by the steps of its furtherance climb ever to loftier things, until the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, and the Lord is seen leaning upon the ladder. Who, I ask, would see this, save one sleeping upon this headrest? who while awake would bring it about that he should stretch out the ladder of his ascent [1112A] as far as heaven, and join the speculation of invisible things to the speculation of visible things? What of this, that upon this path of ascent the play of an angelic meeting offers itself unbidden, so that divine revelation may come to meet human investigation? And so the angels are seen upon this ladder now to ascend, now indeed to descend, and now to instruct the mind toward the highest things, now toward the lowest, so that in things divine and human it may come to know from divine revelation many things which it could not know by itself. And indeed the angels could, without the ministry of a ladder, at the choice of their own desire either descend into the lowest places or fly forth to the highest; nor would there be need for the divine inspiration, in any manifestation of its revelations, to seek the instrument of any bodily likeness, unless it willed that we should see first through [1112B] a glass and in a dark manner, and not at once face to face. And so the angels ascend and descend upon this ladder of likenesses, and some after others now approach, now depart, so that while of the manifold revelations one is brought in and another withdrawn, the mind of the beholder may be illumined in manifold fashion, in order that what it could not grasp all at once, by reason of the slenderness of its understanding, it may understand successively and one by one through intervals of delay. Behold what they find who fall asleep upon this stone. Happy they for whom that is turned into a ladder which for others is wont to be unto ruin. Happy they for whom the knowledge of outward things becomes a ladder of ascent, not a ruin of casting down. Happy they for whom that knowledge which puffs up is not unto puffing up, but unto the inflaming of her that buildeth up. Happy they for whom the beauty of temporal things becomes [1112C] an incitement to eternity. It behooves therefore, as you perceive, him who desires to find this ladder of ascent to lay his head upon the stone, and to harden his mind in the desire of this speculation, and persistently to press upon this pursuit.



## CHAPTER XVII. *On the certainty of discretion.*

We have said that the certainty of discretion is the eleventh stone; and if we seek it diligently, we find it soonest in Paul. For he so trusts in the gift of discretion, he so presumes upon the certainty of his own counsel, that he confidently gives counsel where he has no precept of the Lord: *Concerning virgins,* he says, *I have no precept of the Lord, but I give counsel (I [1112D] Cor. VII)*. Hence it is that he sets himself before others as an example of manner of life, and shows his own life to his followers as a form of living, when he says: *Be ye imitators of me, as I also am of Christ [n: (I Cor. XL)]*. And rightly indeed, in that the Lord set his feet upon a rock and directed his steps. With stones of this kind, as I judge, was the way of those travellers paved concerning whom the Prophet cries out in wonder: *How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, of them that bring glad tidings of good things! [n: (Rom. X.)]* With these stones, unless I am deceived, that great patriarch Joseph, whom the prince of peoples set as lord of his house and prince of all his possession, that he might instruct his princes as his own self, and teach his elders prudence. With these stones, I say, he is rightly believed to have paved the streets of Egypt [1113A], so much so that the children of Israel had no need to serve in clay and brick all the days of their life. The Prophet was still enduring a scarcity of these stones, and was laboring under a great want of discretion, while he was yet fixed in the mire of the deep, because the certainty of a settled counsel was not yet established for him — so much so that he cried out to the Lord and said: *How long shall I take counsels in my soul? [n: (Psal. XVIII.)]* But he would never have fully emerged from this deep of mire, had he not at last at some time found this rock of which we speak: *Upon a rock,* he says, *he hath exalted, me, and now he hath lifted up my head above my enemies [n: (Psal. XXVI)]*. He who does not pave a way for himself out of this kind of stones never walks cleanly, never plants steady steps. He therefore who wishes [1113B] to walk firmly and honorably ought to do nothing at all unadvisedly; and it is plain that he has paved a way for himself with such a stone as he ought, and he can walk securely. Do all things, says the Wise Man, with counsel, and thou shalt never repent [n: (Eccle. XXXII)].



## CHAPTER XVIII. *On the quiet of contemplation.*

The twelfth stone, and the last of all, we can find, as I judge, at the Lord's sepulchre. It has been called, as was said above, [sic: *lapis is*] the tranquillity of contemplation. Of this kind of stones that Joseph of Arimathea hewed out sepulchres for himself; but Jesus, dead, rested in it, because the quiet which prudence seeks for itself through meditation and describes by definition, wisdom finds through contemplation [1113C] and lays hold of by experience. True prudence always seeks, and always ought to seek, that peace which Christ taught, that it may not be troubled nor be afraid. It always strives after where it may find such peace, always endeavors to defend true security for itself; but it always finds something to grieve over out of the past, something to fight against in the present, something to beware of and to dread for the future. The mind, therefore, can shrewdly seek this peace through prudence and subtly investigate it through meditation; yet it will never be able to find it save through wisdom and the grace of contemplation. But when the mind has begun through pure understanding to go beyond its very self, and wholly to enter into that brightness of incorporeal light [1113D], and to draw from the things which it sees in its inmost parts a certain savor of inmost sweetness, and from that to season its own understanding and to turn it into wisdom, then so far, in this excess of mind, is that peace found and obtained which is neither troubled nor afraid, that there is made a silence in heaven as it were for half an hour, so that the mind of the contemplative is troubled by no tumult of contending thoughts: you will find nothing at all which it may either seek through desire, or reprove through disgust, or accuse through hatred. And so he is composed unto the highest peace who is buried in this stone, who is wholly gathered in and shut up within the tranquillity of contemplation. For this stone is not, like that of Jacob, set under the head alone, nor is it, like that later one, spread beneath the feet, but it is fitted and applied to the whole [1114A] body. And so this stone encircles the whole body, encloses the whole, and comprehends it on every side, in that that peace which surpasses all understanding utterly absorbs every human sense, and by a happy transfiguration turns the purer part of the soul into a certain divine habit. Here the body lies without sense and motion in this monument of the Lord; sensuality does nothing, imagination does nothing, and every lower power of the soul is meanwhile clothed with its own office.

For this stone monument does not (as that craggy headrest of the patriarch Jacob does) take up a living body, however lulled asleep, nor does it receive a body unless it be mortified. It is one thing to sleep, another to die. It is one thing to gather one's whole spirit into itself, [1114B] and another to lift it above itself and to forsake oneself. It is one thing to have curbed appetite and to have cut away from the heart the care of outward things, and another that the heart itself should come into forgetfulness of itself. It must be, therefore, before it is permitted to enter into that secret place of inmost quiet and that hidden chamber of the highest tranquillity — it must be, I say, that there take place that very grave and truly wondrous thing: not the dissolution of soul and body, but another far more wondrous and far more glorious than this, that one, in short, of which this is a type, namely the division of soul and spirit. And this, as the Apostle testifies, that living and effectual word of God is wont to work in us, more piercing than any two-edged sword, and reaching unto the division of soul and spirit. What, I ask, anywhere among creatures is discerned more wondrous than this division, where [1114C] that which is essentially one and undivided is cleft into itself, and that which stands simple in itself and without parts is divided and separated from itself? For in one man the essence of his spirit is not one thing and that of his soul another, but altogether one and the same substance, and of a simple nature. For in this twofold term a twofold substance is not understood; but when a twofold power of the same essence is set down for the sake of distinction, the one, the higher, is designated by "spirit," the other, the lower, by "soul." In this division, therefore, the soul and what is animal remains below; but the spirit and what is spiritual flies forth to the heights. What is gross and dreggy fails like a body deadened, and falls back into itself [1114D] and beneath its very self; what is subtle and purged ascends like a spirit breathed forth, and transcends within and beyond its very self. O deep quiet, O sublime rest, where everything that is wont to be moved after a human manner loses all motion, where every motion that then is comes about divinely, and passes over into God! Here that Spirit breathed forth and commended into the hands of the Father does not need a ladder, as did that dreamer Jacob, that it may fly forth to the third — not to say the first — heaven. Why, I ask, should he need a ladder whom the Father bears between his hands, to snatch him to the secrets of the third heaven, so much so that he glories and says: *Thy right hand hath upheld me. Thou hast held my right hand, and by thy will thou hast conducted me, and with glory thou hast received me? [n: (Psal. XVII.)]* That Spirit, therefore, [1115A] taken up out of the midst, has here no need of the office of a ladder, nor does it need in that ascent of its own subtlety to be supported by the shadowing forth of any bodily likeness, where it sees face to face, not through a glass and in a dark manner. I lie, if they themselves who are of this kind do not assert the same concerning themselves: *But we all,* they say, *beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from brightness to brightness, as by the Spirit of the Lord [n: (II Cor. III)]*. You surely see what it does, and you understand, as I judge, what that division of soul and spirit avails, of which we have already spoken above. The spirit is divided from the lowest things that it may be raised to the highest. The spirit is cleft from the soul that it may be united to the Lord. For he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit. Happy division, and separation to be longed for, where that which [1115B] is discerned to be passible, to be corruptible, meanwhile dies to its own passions, so far that nothing of passibility, nothing of corruptibility is meanwhile felt; where also that which is spiritual, which is subtle, is raised up even to the speculation of the divine glory, and is transformed into the same image. The lower part, therefore, is composed unto the highest peace and tranquillity, but the higher part is raised up unto glory and gladness. So we have recognized that the face of Moses (the higher part indeed of the body) was glorified from fellowship with the Lord, so that the children of Israel could not look upon his countenance because of its brightness. Who, I ask, would suffice worthily to tell, who to unfold, what of perfection the spirit acquires in the glorification of its own excess, [1115C] although it does not extend the prolonging of its pilgrimage as far as the third day, even if it does not draw out the delay of silence as far as half an hour, [1116A] granted that it goes and returns after the likeness of flashing lightning? So Moses brings back from the fellowship of the divine converse, together with a glorified countenance, horns also, showing what of power, what of strength he had drawn from companionship with him who gives power and strength to his people, the blessed God. That spirit therefore at last returns and comes back to itself which had gone far beyond itself; and what it had laid aside as passible and corruptible it takes up again as it were impassible and incorruptible, by comparison with its former state, and rises again into newness of life. What does it seem to you, to grow cheerful at an injury inflicted, not to blush at a contumely cast in one's teeth, to rejoice over tribulation? is not this to walk in newness of life, and after some manner to show oneself impassible, and not to lie subject [1116B] to one's own passions? Behold how far they advance who rest in this stone. There are many things which could have been said concerning this matter, if they ought to have been said in this place and did not exceed the measure of a moderate digression. For I think this last kind of stones to be the most worthy and most precious of all. Yet we ought to despise none, but to seek at least single ones out of the single kinds, and to gather them into one.

It is indeed to be noted that this is the first work which is commanded to be done in the land of promise, so that an eternal memorial of the divine works may be established first of all. For without this mound of stones that promise of the Lord of an eternal inheritance is never bravely acquired, never securely possessed. For he who forgets the benefits [1116C] divinely received does not deserve to be advanced to the obtaining of greater things.
